term_table.lsj_entry_text: παρακμ-ή, ἡ, point at which the prime is past, decay, Plu. 2.453b ; σώματος Ph. Fr. 97 H.; φθινοπώρου Sch. Arat. 1082 ; π. τῆς νόσου abatement, Plu. Marc. 24 , cf. S.E. P. 2.238 : metaph., of numbers, Iamb. in Nic. p.77 P.
term_table.lsj_first_sense_gloss: point at which the prime is past
term_table.greek_sentence: εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἐξαρκέσει τῷ τῆς ἀκμῆς καιρῷ καὶ χωρὶς τοῦ τροφὴν προσενέγκασθαι, κράτιστον ἀσιτεῖν ἄχρι τοῦ τὴν παρακμὴν ἀπάρξασθαι· εἰ δ’ οὐχ οἷόν τε ἀσιτοῦντα διαρκέσαι, θρεπτέον αὐτὸν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς εὐθέως ἐν ἅπαντι καιρῷ τῷ δυναμένῳ προσδέξασθαι τροφὴν, ἔστι δὲ οὗτος ὁ τῆς ἀνέσεως.
term_table.english_sentence_A: For if it will hold out until the time of the acme even without taking nourishment, it is best to abstain from food until the decline has begun; but if it is not possible for him to last while fasting, he must be nourished right from the beginning at every period that is able to receive nourishment, and this is the period of remission.
term_table.english_sentence_B: For if it will hold out through the time of the peak even without taking food, it is best to fast until the decline has begun; but if he cannot last out while fasting, he must be fed right from the beginning at every period able to receive food, and this is the period of remission.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἄνεσις, gen. εως, Ion. ιος , ἡ: (ἀνιημι):— loosening, relaxing, τῶν χορδῶν of the strings, opp. ἐπίτασις, Pl. R. 349e ; coupled with χάλασις, ib. 590b ; τῆς αἰσθήσεως . . δεσμὸν τὸν ὕπνον εἶναί φαμεν, τὴν δέ . . ἄνεσιν ἐγρήγορσιν Arist. Somn.Vig. 454b27 ; ἀέρος Thphr. CP 2.1.6 ; πάγων ἄ., i.e. a thaw, Plu. Sert. 17 ; of the ebb-tide, Str. 7.2.1 . metaph., remission, abatement, κακῶν Hdt. 5.28 ; opp. θλῖψις, 2 Ep.Cor. 8.13 , al.; λύπης, μοχθηρίας, etc., Plu. 2.102b , etc.; τὴν ἡδονὴν ἄνεσιν λαμβάνειν Phld. D. 3 Fr. 1 ; ἄ. φόρων, τελῶν, remission of tribute, taxes, Plu. Sert. 6 , IG 7.2227 (Thisbe), etc.; κολάσεως Plot. 4.3.24 ; of fevers, opp. παροξυσμός, Gal. 7.427 . relaxation, recreation, opp. σπουδή, Pl. Lg. 724a , Arist. Rh. 1371b34 , cf. Cleanth.Stoic. 1.122 ; ἄ. καὶ σχολή Plb. 1.66.10 ; ψυχῆς Mnesith.Ath. ap. Ath. 11.484a . solution, Dsc. 5.96 . = τὸ τελευταῖον τῆς παρακμῆς Archig. ap. Gal. 7.424 . indulgence, licence, ἡδονῶν Pl. R. 561a ; ἡ τῶν γυναικῶν παρ' ὑμῖν ἄ. Id. Lg. 637c , cf. Arist. Pol. 1270a1 ; δούλων ib. 1313b35 ; relaxation of custody, Act.Ap. 24.23 . of musical pitch, Aristid.Quint. 1.5 ; of an unaccented syll., Phld. Po. 2.18 .
term_table.greek_sentence: λέγω δὲ ἄνεσιν ἄρτι τὸ δεύτερον μόριον τῆς ὅλης περιόδου διαιρεθείσης εἰς δύο τὰ πάντα, παροξυσμόν τε καὶ ἄνεσιν.
term_table.english_sentence_A: I call remission here the second part of the whole cycle divided into two in all, paroxysm and remission.
term_table.english_sentence_B: By remission I mean here the second part of the whole period, when the whole is divided into two, paroxysm and remission.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἀγαθός [αγ], ή, όν, Lacon. ἀγασός Ar. Lys. 1301 , Cypr. ἀζαθός GDI 57 :— good: of persons, well-born, gentle, opp. κακός, δειλός, οἷά τε τοῖς ἀγαθοῖσι παραδρώωσι χέρηες Od. 15.324 , cf. Il. 1.275 ; ἀφνειός τ' ἀ. τε Il. 13.664 , cf. Od. 18.276 ; πατρὸς δ' εἴμ' ἀγαθοῖο, θεὰ δέ με γείνατο μήτηρ Il. 21.109 , cf. Od. 4.611 ; κακὸς ἐξ ἀ. Thgn. 190 , cf. 57 sq.; πραῢς ἀστοῖς, οὐ φθονέων ἀγαθοῖς Pi. P. 3.71 , cf. 2.96 , 4.285 ; τίς ἂν εὔπατρις ὧδε βλάστοι; οὐδεὶς τῶν ἀ. κτλ. S. El. 1082 ; οἵ τ' ἀ. πρὸς τῶν ἀγενῶν κατανικῶνται Id. Fr. 84 ; τοὺς εὐγενεῖς γὰρ κἀγαθοὺς . . φιλεῖ Ἄρης ἐναίρειν ib. 649 , cf. E. Alc. 600 , al.: ἀγαθοὶ καὶ ἐξ ἀγαθῶν Pl. Phdr. 274a :—in political sense, aristocrats, esp. in the phrase καλοὶ κἀγαθοί (v. sub καλοκἀγαθός). brave, valiant, since courage was attributed to Chiefs and Nobles, Il. 1.131 , al.; τῷ κ' ἀγαθὸς μὲν ἔπεφν', ἀγαθὸν δέ κεν ἐξενάριξεν 21.280 ; cf. Hdt. 5.109 , etc. good, capable, in reference to ability, ἀ. βασιλεύς Il. 3.179 ; ἰητήρ 2.732 ; θεράπων 16.165 , 17.388 ; πύκτης Xenoph. 2.15 ; ἰητρός Hp. Prog. 1 ; προβατογνώμων A. Ag. 795 ; ἄρχοντες Democr. 266 : freq. with qualifying words, ἀ. ἐν ὑσμίνῃ Il. 13.314 ; βοὴν ἀ. 2.408 , 563 , al.; πύξ Od. 11.300 ; βίην Il. 6.478 ; γνώμην S. OT 687 ; πᾶσαν ἀρετήν Pl. Lg. 899b , cf. Alc. 1.124e ; τέχνην Id. Prt. 323b ; τὰ πολέμια, τὰ πολιτικά, Hdt. 9.122 , Pl. Grg. 516b , etc.: more rarely c. dat., ἀ. πολέμῳ X. Oec. 4.15 : with Preps., ἄνδρες ἀ. περὶ τὸ πλῆθος Lys. 13.2 ; εἴς τι Pl. Alc. 1.125a ; πρός τι Id. R. 407e : c. inf., ἀ. μάχεσθαι Hdt. 1.136 ; ἱππεύεσθαι 1.79 ; ἀ. ἱστάναι good at weighing, Pl. Prt. 356b . good, in moral sense, first in Thgn. 438 , cf. Heraclit. 104 , S. El. 1082 , X. Mem. 1.7.1 , Pl. Ap. 41d , etc.; ψυχῆς ἀγαθῆς πατρὶς ὁ ξύμπας κόσμος Democr. 247 : freq. with other Adjs., ὁ πιστὸς κἀ. S. Tr. 541 ; δικαίων κἀ. ib. 1050 :—ironical, τὸν ἀ. Κρέοντα Id. Ant. 31 . ὦ ἀγαθέ, my good friend, as a term of gentle remonstrance, Pl. Prt. 311a , etc. ἀ. δαίμων, v. sub δαίμων; ἀ. τύχη, v. sub τύχη; ἀ. θεός = Lat. bona dea, Plu. Caes. 9 , Cic. 19 . of things, good, serviceable, Ἰθάκη . . ἀ. κουροτρόφος Od. 9.27 , etc.; ἀ. τοῖς τοκεῦσι, τῇ πόλει X. Cyn. 13.17 : c. gen., εἴ τι οἶδα πυρετοῦ ἀ. good for it, Id. Mem. 3.8.3 ; ἑλκῶν Thphr. HP 9.11.1 . of outward circumstances, αἰδὼς οὐκ ἀ. κεχρημένῳ ἀνδρὶ παρεῖναι Od. 17.347 ; εἰπεῖν εἰς ἀγαθόν to good purpose, Il. 9.102 ; ὁ δὲ πείσεται εἰς ἀ. περ for his own good end, 11.789 ; οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη 2.204 :—ἀγαθόν [ἐστι], c. inf., it is good to do so and so<*> Il. 7.282 , 24.130 , Od. 3.196 , etc. morally good, πρῆξις Democr. 177 ; ἔργα Emp. 112.2 , cf. Ep.Rom. 2.7 , etc. ἀγαθόν, τό, good, blessing, benefit, of persons or things, ὦ μέγα ἀ. σὺ τοῖς φίλοις X. Cyr. 5.3.20 ; φίλον, ὃ μέγιστον ἀ. εἶναί φασι Id. Mem. 2.4.2 , cf. Ar. Ra. 74 , etc; as term of endearment for a baby, blessing!, treasure!, Men. Sam. 28 :— ἀγαθόν τινα δεδρακέναι, πεποιηκέναι confer a benefit on . . , Th. 3.68 , Lys. 13.92 ; ἐπ' ἀγαθῷ τινος for one's good, Th. 5.27 , X. Cyr. 7.4.3 ; ἐπ' ἀ. τοῖς πολίταις Ar. Ra. 1487 ; οὐκ ἐπ' ἀ. for no good end, Th. 1.131 ; ἐπ' οὐδενὶ ἀ. τῆς Ἑλλάδος X. HG 5.2.35 :—in pl., ἡ ἐπ' ἀγαθοῖς γεναμένη (sic) κατασπορά PFlor. 21.10 (iii A.D.):—τὸ ἀ. or τἀ., the good, Epich. 171.5 , cf. Pl. R. 506b , 508e , Arist. Metaph. 1091a31 , etc.:—in pl., ἀγαθά, τά, goods of fortune, treasures, wealth, Hdt. 2.172 , Lys. 13.91 , X. Mem. 1.2.63 , etc.; ἀγαθὰ πράττειν fare well, Ar. Av. 1706 ; also, good things, dainties, Thgn. 1000 , Ar. Ach. 873 , etc.: good qualities, τοῖς ἀ., οἷς ἔχομεν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ Isoc. 8.32 , cf. Democr. 37 ; good points, of a horse, εἰ τἄλλα πάντα ἀ. ἔχοι, κακόπους δ' εἴη X. Eq. 1.2 . Comp. and Sup. are usu. supplied from other stems, viz. Comp. ἀμείνων, ἀρείων<*> βελτίων, κρείσσων ʽκάρρωνʼ, λωΐων (λώʽωνʼ), Ep. βέλτερος, λωΐτερος, φέρτερος:— Sup. ἄριστος, βέλτιστος, κράτιστος, λώϊστος (λῷστος), Ep. βέλτατος, κάρτιστος, φέρτατος, φέριστος:— later, reg. Comp. ἀγαθώτερος LXX Jd. 11.25 , 15.2 , D.S. 8 Fr. 12 , Plot. 5.5.9 , Diod.Rh. p.53.9H. : Sup. ἀγαθώτατος D.S. 16.85 , Hld. 5.15 , etc. ( -ότατος POxy. 1757.26 (ii A.D.)). Adv. usually εὖ, q.v.: ἀγαθῶς Hp. Off. 9 , Arist. Rh. 1388b6 , LXX 1 Ki. 20.7 . (Etym. dub. ( ὅτι ἄγει ἡμᾶς ἐπὶ τὸν ὀρθὸν βίον Stoic. 3.49 ); perh. cognate with ἄγαμαι, hence admirable.)
term_table.greek_sentence: Ἱπποκράτης μὲν οὖν πάντων πρῶτος ὧν ἴσμεν ὀρθῶς περὶ τούτου διωρίσατο· βέλτιον δὲ ἂν ἐξεργάσασθαι τὴν τέχνην αὐτοῦ· σχεδὸν δὲ οὐδεὶς τοῦτο ἐποίησεν, ἔνιοι δὲ καὶ τελέως ἀποχωρήσαντες αὐτῆς εἰς μακρολογίαν ἐξετράποντο, καθάπερ καὶ Ἀρχιγένης ἔν τε τοῖς ἄλλοις ἅπασι κᾀν τοῖς δύο βιβλίοις, ἃ περὶ τῶν ἐν ταῖς νόσοις καιρῶν ἐγράψατο.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Hippocrates, then, first of all those we know, correctly made the distinctions concerning this; but it would have been better to work out his art further; yet practically no one has done this, and some, having departed from it entirely, turned aside into prolixity, as did Archigenes both in all his other writings and in the two books which he wrote on the periods in diseases.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Hippocrates, then, first of all those we know of, made correct determinations about this; but it would have been better to work out his art more fully. Yet almost no one did this, and some, departing from it altogether, turned aside into prolixity, as Archigenes did both in all his other writings and in the two books which he wrote on the periods in diseases.

term_table.lsj_entry_text: ἔνιοι, αι, α, some; never in Ep. , Lyr., or Att. Poets before Men. , exc. Ar. Pl. 867 (cf. however ἐνίοτε); first used in Ion. Prose, as Hdt. 1.120 , 8.56 , Hp. Praec. 6 ; πολλοὶ μὲν . . ἔνιοι δὲ . . Lys. 25.19 ; ἔνιοι μὲν . . ἔνιοι δὲ . . Pl. Tht. 151a , X. Mem. 4.2.38 ; ἔνιοι μὲν . . οἱ δὲ . . Pl. Mx. 238e ; ἔνιοί τινες Isoc. 15.258 : later in sg., οὐ πᾶσα κίνησις θερμαίνει, ἀλλ' ἐνία ψύχει Arist. Pr. 884b13 , cf. Thphr. Vert. 1 ; περὶ ψυχῆς ἐνίας θεωρῆσαι Arist. Metaph. 1026a5 : neut. pl. as Adv., συμμανῆναι ἔνια δεῖ Men. 421 ; ἔστι καὶ ταὐτόματον ἔνια χρήσιμον Id. 486 .
term_table.greek_sentence: Ἱπποκράτης μὲν οὖν πάντων πρῶτος ὧν ἴσμεν ὀρθῶς περὶ τούτου διωρίσατο· βέλτιον δὲ ἂν ἐξεργάσασθαι τὴν τέχνην αὐτοῦ· σχεδὸν δὲ οὐδεὶς τοῦτο ἐποίησεν, ἔνιοι δὲ καὶ τελέως ἀποχωρήσαντες αὐτῆς εἰς μακρολογίαν ἐξετράποντο, καθάπερ καὶ Ἀρχιγένης ἔν τε τοῖς ἄλλοις ἅπασι κᾀν τοῖς δύο βιβλίοις, ἃ περὶ τῶν ἐν ταῖς νόσοις καιρῶν ἐγράψατο.
term_table.english_sentence_A: Hippocrates, then, first of all those we know, correctly made the distinctions concerning this; but it would have been better to work out his art further; yet practically no one has done this, and some, having departed from it entirely, turned aside into prolixity, as did Archigenes both in all his other writings and in the two books which he wrote on the periods in diseases.
term_table.english_sentence_B: Hippocrates, then, first of all those we know of, made correct determinations about this; but it would have been better to work out his art more fully. Yet almost no one did this, and some, departing from it altogether, turned aside into prolixity, as Archigenes did both in all his other writings and in the two books which he wrote on the periods in diseases.

A.translation: [440] GALEN'S BOOK ON THE PERIODS OF THE WHOLE DISEASE. Of the whole disease, then, we conceive periods analogous to the ages of living beings: one, and the first, that of its generation; a second, that of its increase; a third, that of its acme; and a fourth, that of its decline, at any rate whenever the patients are going to be saved; for if they have died first, either during the increase or the acme, it is quite evident that such a disease has not passed through all the periods.

But the disease that does run through them all admits disputes concerning almost all of its parts: some saying that the acme is a single point of time, [441] grasped by conception alone; some that, as in the synochous fevers, there is no acme at all; some bringing the acme into a beginning of short duration; others removing the beginning, not only in these but in all the remaining diseases as well; and others sometimes removing the decline too, if the disease is resolved by "cutting off" (apokopē), as they call it. First, then, these disputes must be resolved; next, the concepts of the periods of the whole disease must be precisely articulated; after this their distinguishing signs must be stated; and then in turn it would be in order to show their usefulness, mingling them with the matters concerning the circuits. The beginning of the disease, then, insofar as it at some point sets in when the healthy condition collapses, is in all of them conceived of without any extension of time; along with this, however, it is not granted that every disease has, as it were, a generation, in the way we conceive of it in the case of animals. For diseases are not composed out of certain parts in the way that the animal is composed of head, thorax, and limbs.

For falling away [442] from the natural state, they have their coming-to-be in some instant of time, and from there they ascend up to the acme. For let the disease be, say, one consisting in a dyscrasia, in accordance with which, as has been demonstrated by us, fever too is constituted. It is necessary, then, that as soon as this heat contrary to nature first arises, the man is in fever, and that the heat is intensified up to the acme. For of that which has no parts, how could there be a coming-to-be in time? These things were stated by me right at the beginning too, and I replied to them, by recalling the fevers that make their attack with chilling. But in the case of the periods the reply is sufficient; for the time of the chilling is one of the partial times of the whole disease and first in order; but it would be most ridiculous to regard the first time of the first paroxysm as the beginning of the whole disease. For indeed this time, which they name the beginning of the disease, possesses its usefulness with regard to remedies, and looking to this he said: "When diseases are beginning, if anything seems to need moving, move it; but when they are at their acme, it is better to keep quiet."

And likewise that too has been said by him: [443] "Around the beginnings and the ends all things are weaker." And indeed also what has been said about purging by drugs, that one must purge and move what is concocted, not what is crude, nor at the beginnings, unless it is in turgescence. And in addition to these, further, the saying: "In acute affections use purging drugs rarely, and at the beginnings." And many other things besides these, some said by Hippocrates, some by all the other ancient physicians, do not permit us to understand the beginning as the onset of the first paroxysm, but as extending over a longer time, such that one is able both to let blood and to use a clyster, and sometimes, if it is urgent, also to purge—in addition to its being ridiculous to posit the same beginning for the diseases that are resolved within the seventh day and for those that persist for a year, as the quartan sometimes does. Many things, then, have been said by me about this beginning also in the first book of On Crises, where I showed how one might recognize this first period; and its chief point was the lack of concoction of the disease. But it is better here too to say, in addition to those things, whatever is useful for the present exposition.

[444] Let it be laid down first, then, that the beginning of an inflammation is what is being sought. Who would not say that its generation, as it were, exists in that whole time during which the part is being filled with blood-like substance? For whether such a thing comes about through paremptosis (παρεμπτώσει), or through the wedging-in (σφηνώσει) of all the vessels, or through some blocking (περιστάσει) of the masses in the pores, or whether, as we taught both in the treatise On Uneven Dyskrasia and in that On Tumours contrary to Nature, some excess of blood is formed in the part as the inflammation is being generated, this will be the first period, in which the part is being filled, in correspondence (ἀνακείμενον) with the magnitude of the affection. But when that which flows in ceases, and what is contained in the inflamed part begins to putrefy, a certain heat arises on account of the putrefaction, and the diffusion increases further on account of the heat, upon which pneuma too is generated, and because of both of these the part is distended more than before, even if nothing should flow in; this is the second time, that of the increase of the inflammation.

But when it is already changing into pus, then indeed the greatest pains [445] take hold. For the pains and the fevers occur around the generation of the pus rather than once it has been generated; and such a period is called the acme of the affection. But if the flux, by suppurating or being dispersed, renders the swelling and the tension less, such a condition is the beginning of the decline. In this way, then, the periods are divided in the case of inflammation. In the case of fever, for the one that arises upon an inflammation, one should posit the same periods as for the inflammation; but for the one that arises upon a humour without inflammation, the time of the non-concoction of the offending humours is the beginning; and when they begin to be concocted, the beginning has ceased and the second period has arrived, the one named that of the ascent; and when the concoction itself is being accomplished most fully, that of the acme; then, next, that of the decline, in which both the magnitude of the symptoms and the abundance of the things being concocted have already ceased, but there is still a small remnant of the humours that need to be concocted.

And I have shown in the treatise On Crises also all the signs, both those of faint concoction and those of complete non-concoction, and those of manifest and those of perfect [concoction], [446] some being peculiar to the concoctions in the belly, others peculiar to those in the veins, and still others peculiar to those of the respiratory parts. And some were taken from the stools, others from the urines, others from the sputa. And I went through these at very great length in that work together with the Hippocratic passages; but in the present discussion it suffices to say only this much, that the periods of ulcers too are the same. For first watery, unconcocted and thin ichors flow from them; then next they are less in amount and thicker; and then at that point thin pus; then this becomes less in quantity but thicker and whiter; so that there is none of the affections that undergo resolution which does not pass through the periods. Nor indeed does the knowledge of them come from anything else than the signs of non-concoction and concoction, which are recognised through the residues. For who does not know that the belly has failed to concoct, having seen stools that are unchylified (ἀχύλωτα)? And who does not know, having seen watery urine, that the concoction in the vessels has miscarried?

And who, having seen thin sputum coughed up in pleuritis or peripneumonia, will not likewise understand that it is still the beginning [447] of the affection? So too in ophthalmias: at the beginning what flows off is copious and thin, quite unconcocted; next, it is less and thicker, taking on some outline of concoction; then, as time advances, the quantity diminishing and the consistency proceeding toward the thicker, the signs of concoction increase to such a degree that the eyelids of those who have slept are even glued together by the rheum (lēmē) that has formed, which itself too, being at first thin and copious, but with time becoming less and thicker, indicates both the concoction of the disease and its decline. And indeed, of the things that flow down from the brain through the palate and the nostrils, the beginning is when what is carried down is watery and thin and copious and acrid; for these things indicate extreme lack of concoction; but it is already a mark of concoction when what is evacuated is thicker and less acrid and small in amount; and if what is called mucus (myxa) and phlegm (blenna) also pass out together with it, this is now a surer sign of concoction; just as indeed also, (if) it becomes thicker than it was and less, it indicates concoction much more still. And these are the periods of the diseases from which the sick are saved.

[448] Concerning the others, in which the patients perish, I shall speak a little later, having first articulated those of the things said which require some distinction. One of these, then, is also the question concerning the acme: whether it is always without duration, so far as depends on itself, even if to perception it often appears to be extended over considerable periods of time; or whether it always has some breadth, at one time greater, at another less; or whether in some diseases it has duration, while in others it is without duration. But since the inquiry requires a longer discussion, I am inclined to pass over it entirely, imitating Hippocrates, who said concerning the dislocation at the shoulder: "I, for my part, do not insist upon this, although I have something I could say." For just as he was content with what he had always observed, in the same way I too shall now speak as one who has always seen it so. I have observed every acme of the individual paroxysms to come about over a period of time, so that even if with respect to its nature it were without duration, we derive no use from that fact.

For when the decline first becomes clear to perception, then we employ the remedies that suit it; [449] but so long as the magnitude of the fever stands at equal measures (ἀπὸ τῶν ἴσων ἀριθμῶν), for so long it is fitting to do what is proper to the magnitude of the acme. In the same way, in ophthalmia and pleuritis and every inflammation and each of the other diseases, the general periods dictate the use of the different remedies, being measured by perception. The inquiry about the breadth of the acme, then, becomes a logical one, whether one were to examine it with regard to the particular paroxysms or with regard to the whole disease; but at present it is not my purpose to draw distinctions about such matters, as those do who bring everything into everything, one of whom is Archigenes. For this man mixes into the most strictly medical treatises sometimes an inquiry about names, and sometimes one about the things themselves, but a logical one; whereas we, just as we have always guarded against this, shall act in the same way now too: leaving it to others to inquire about the acme, whether it is without duration or with some duration, we shall measure its usefulness, seeing clearly that the acmastic nature, both in the ages of life, is dissolved over a broad span of time, and in diseases sometimes over a longer, often over a shorter, but in any case over a perceptible one.

[450] This very difference of time is clearer to observe in the case of the age at its acme in animals; for indeed we see hunting dogs and racing horses already performing some work proper to them in the period of growth, and after this we say that they have become mature, and we see clearly that they are stronger than before, and that they remain equally strong not for one year only, but also for two and sometimes even three years; just as also human athletes who have remained equal in strength, so far as perception goes, not for these three years only, but often for four and five. So too, as I said, in diseases as well the particular paroxysms produce their acmes in a clearly perceptible time, and much more do the general periods of the whole disease have breadth, both all the others and that of the acme no less (is) than each of the others. And it is possible sometimes to recognize them clearly, sometimes dimly, or even to be wholly ignorant of them for a very long time.

And on this account some diseases seem to attack at once at their acme; yet this very thing is among the impossibilities, for not even [451] the so-called synochos (continuous) fever ever attacked immediately from its acme, but from the first onset to the most complete acme it arrives in four or three hours at the very least, and from then on it remains altogether equal to itself continuously until the crisis. But neither could one say that what attacks most suddenly of all, apoplexy, attacks at its acme; for such a thing is not strictly the case, but rather it passes through its beginning and its increase in a short time; yet it is not without a beginning, nor does it attack at once in its most complete form, just as neither does the paroxysm of epilepsy. For no one is seized so suddenly by the symptom as those who have their neck cut off; and yet even in their case the cut has a first portion of time and a second and a third and a fourth, just as if some surgeon were cutting anything whatever. But still, if you wish, let it be granted that the epileptic and the apoplectic collapse occur without time, so that I may go through what I set out from the beginning.

For this itself—the collapse that occurs—is a symptom; but the disease is not this, rather it must in every case be, as we have demonstrated, some disposition [452] of the body. And if we possess no sign either of its coming into being or of its increasing, this does not overturn the consequent argument, according to which we were saying that it is necessary for every disease to arrive at its acme through the increase; rather, it concedes that the increase of diseases is sometimes hard to recognize and, for many, unrecognizable. That what I say is true, I could persuade you by this very brief argument. I have often observed scirrhous swellings in the legs forming right from the beginning without an inflammation having preceded them, and increasing little by little over three and sometimes even four years, without perceptibly impeding the necessary activities of the leg; but in the course of time, owing to their considerable size, at some later point troubling even the walking.

Conceive, then—for it is not impossible—that in the concave parts of the liver some scirrhous tumour is already forming; and its formation will escape notice up to a certain point, though later the features of the disposition itself will become more evident, while not even then are we able to discover in what disposition this occurs; and some time later, at some point, a hydropic effusion [453] will also supervene, the scirrhous tumour not even then giving any indication to the touch; but later at least, having appeared of notable size, it reminded us of our previous ignorance. At any rate I have seen not a few who, along such a course of symptoms, in a short time brought to light a not small tumour in a scirrhous liver, one that had been forming for a long time but had escaped notice on account of its smallness and the good nourishment of the muscles in the hypochondrium. But when the scirrhus, as it grows, at once mounts up to the convex parts of the liver and at the same time becomes the cause of atrophy both to the other parts of the animal and to the muscles in the hypochondrium, from both of these you will clearly diagnose it in a short time, it having already attained a notable size. All such matters, indeed, are connected with the examination of the affected parts, which it is not our purpose to investigate at present, but what has been shown concerning their association has not been without use. But it is time to go on to the argument from the beginning.

For each of the diseases there is a proper period, that of its generation, sometimes perceptible, sometimes not perceptible; after which, in turn, comes that of the increase, and this too is not perceptible in all cases alike; [454] upon which there follows that of the acme, which is perceptible in every case, while we admit that sometimes we have no clear sign of the beginning of the affection and of its increase. In these cases, then, so far as concerns the use of the art, one will truly say that only the period of the acme exists; but if the patients are also going to be saved, the period of the decline follows upon it in every case, perceptible, and such as to be constituted in a time that is not without breadth (οὐκ ἀπλατεῖ). For even if someone should be brought to crisis swiftly either through hemorrhage or through sweats, there is at any rate for this person too some perceptible period, that of the decline; and if this is shorter than that which occurs in other diseases, which decline over three or four or even more days, this evidently in no way harms the preceding argument, nor does it discredit the chief point of the assertion, but it still stands: that in all diseases which are resolved there is, just as an acme, so also some decline. These matters having been sufficiently demonstrated by us, we shall next examine the diseases which are not resolved.

Their nature is twofold. For some of them have their constitution, [455] when they have it completely brought to fulfilment; others belong to the nature of diseases that are resolved, but when they succeed in killing first, it happens to them in this respect [not to be resolved]. And of these too the manner is threefold: for either on account of the weakness of the patient, or on account of the strength of the diseases, or on account of both together, it destroys [the patient] before being resolved. But on another account there is one common type of all such cases, when it is beyond the capacity [of the patient]; for indeed the very thing that holds together the destruction of the patient is placed in this: that no one can be saved unless nature prevails over the disease, nor perish without nature being defeated and the disease becoming the stronger over it. And for this very reason some suppose that one single thing is signified by 'great disease', it being constituted in the category of relation, not knowing that 'great disease' is indeed sometimes said in this way too, just as if we were to say 'greater', when it is beyond the capacity; but it is also said in respect of its own substance, as a man, or a horse, or an ox is great.

And concerning this twofold signification too demonstration has already been given by me many times in other works; but to work out everything in every treatise is [456] idle talk; so I shall say what is useful for the present purpose. Each of the diseases possesses in and of itself a certain magnitude (for it is better to put it thus for the sake of clarity), and this magnitude of the disease is either beyond the faculty, so as to weigh it down, or, on the contrary, weaker than the faculty, so as to be overcome by it, provided all things are done well. So when it is beyond the faculty, the person will in every case die. In that case the periods of the disease are in one respect taken in the same way as those mentioned before, in another respect not in the same way. For the beginning has its constitution in the same manner, in the generation of the disease; but the increase lies not in concoction, as in the case of those who are going to be saved, but in the signs of lack of concoction and the deadly signs. For it was shown, if we remember at all, that these differ from one another; but for the sake of recollection some of them will be stated now as well.

Well-coloured urine, then, that is moderately thick is the finest of all urines, so far as colour and consistency are concerned; but there must in every case be present along with it either a good suspended matter (enaiōrēma), [457] or a cloud, or a sediment, as the nature of the disease demands; for we showed that the sediments come about in one way in bilious diseases and in another in the plethoras arising from crude humours. Diametrically opposite, as one might say, is the unconcocted urine, which has neither suspended matter nor sediment nor cloud, and which, moreover, has not taken on any thickness or yellowness, but is white in colour and thin in consistency, like water; if, however, some black cloud, or black suspended matter, or black sediment should arise in it, and still more if the whole of it should be dusky, it is deadly; just as also if bran-like or scale-like particles should appear in it; and indeed, urine that is strongly foul-smelling, and that which is fatty, which they call oily, is deadly. These, then, are the urines that are marks of a great disease, one which, I was saying, is great according to its own nature.

And it is great also if the sputum in pleuritic and peripneumonic patients is either black, or intensely fiery-red, or frothy, or considerably foul-smelling, or not expectorated at all, while a strong pain or difficulty of breathing [458] holds the person in its grip. Analogous to these there is also, in the other diseases, all those that are constituted in the liver or the stomach, a class of deadly signs, whence it is not even possible to define the acme in such diseases in a manner similar to the acme of those who are going to be saved; for there the greatest paroxysms delimited the acme, but here it is not possible to define the greatest ones in like manner, since the disease is not being concocted at all; rather one must grasp by conception the greatest point, to which the disease sometimes arrives, while sometimes it kills beforehand. In the case, at any rate, of an inflammation that is being resolved, the generation of pus is the boundary of the acme; but in the case of one that is not going to be resolved, it is possible for the person to die even during its increase; and it is also possible for the faculty, if it is very strong, to hold out until the final magnitude. For indeed the greatest magnitude of this inflammation, whenever it is not going to be resolved, ends either in gangrene or in putrefaction; and so long as there is not yet any of these, it is possible for it to be increased.

And let the increases in each genus of the other diseases [459] be understood analogously to the inflammation. Not only their genera, but also their differentiae and their species, have been set out in a single treatise, which is entitled On the Differentiae of Diseases. But I ask you to direct your mind most of all to that point which, if overlooked, could considerably trip someone up. For it is possible for a man to be held at one and the same time by both two and three diseases, of which one is already declining, another still remains in the period of its beginning or in the first stages of its increase, and another has increased to its greatest extent; and then for the man to die, neither on account of the one that is declining, nor on account of the one that is now beginning, but on account of the one that has greatly increased. Above all, then, examine the three sources of the faculties that govern the whole body, how they are disposed—I mean these: brain, heart and liver; and next also all the other parts, those that grow out from each of the sources—nerves, veins and arteries—and whatever parts possess a nature of their own but are governed by all the sources, some on equal terms, some more by one and less by another.

[460] For from such an investigation you will discover, first, whether there is one disease or several in the person; then, next, examine the proper periods of each, since these are necessary for the discovery of the remedies, for the sake of which this discourse of ours is being pursued. For about the beginnings and the ends everything is weaker, about the acmes stronger, and between these, whatever lies between. For the things nearer the beginning are weaker than those nearer the acme, just as also are the things nearer the end; and those equidistant from the beginning and the acme are intermediate in strength between both extremes; and so too those equidistant from the acme and the termination, these too are intermediate between their own extremes.

In treatment, then, the soothing element ought to prevail at the acme, while at the beginning and at the end the combative element; and let the intermediate periods be taken in proportion to the extremes, as has been said at greater length in the treatise on the therapeutic method; but now I have gone through only the main heads themselves, so far as suffices for an outline, indicating the usefulness of the distinction in diseases according to [461] periods. For it is not possible to discover how one is to regulate the regimen, nor when one is to give nourishment, without determining these securely — if indeed one must conjecture, right at the beginning, both when the acme of the disease will be and how great the strength of the patient is. For if it will hold out until the time of the acme even without taking nourishment, it is best to abstain from food until the decline has begun; but if it is not possible for him to last while fasting, he must be nourished right from the beginning at every period that is able to receive nourishment, and this is the period of remission. I call remission here the second part of the whole cycle divided into two in all, paroxysm and remission. Hippocrates, then, first of all those we know, correctly made the distinctions concerning this; but it would have been better to work out his art further; yet practically no one has done this, and some, having departed from it entirely, turned aside into prolixity, as did Archigenes both in all his other writings and in the two books which he wrote on the periods in diseases.

You will learn clearly what I mean by examining these two things carefully: [462] one, whether these things that have now been said by us throughout this whole book are most useful for treatment and prognosis; the other, whether anything has been said by Archigenes. For if, with nothing lacking in these, he is seen to say other things, he errs doubly, both in not teaching what is useful and in burdening those who read his books with the verbosity of useless matters.

B.translation: [440] GALEN'S BOOK ON THE PERIODS OF THE WHOLE DISEASE. Of the whole disease, then, we conceive periods analogous to the ages of living beings: one, the first, that of its genesis; the second, that of its increase; the third, that of its peak; and the fourth, that of its decline, at least when the patients are going to be saved. For if they die before this, either during the increase or at the peak, it is quite clear that such a disease has not passed through all the periods.

But the disease that does pass through them all is disputed with regard to practically every one of its parts. Some say that the peak is a single moment of time [441], grasped by conception alone; others, that in the continuous fevers (synochoi) there is no peak at all; others introduce the peak into a beginning of short duration; others take away the beginning, not only in these but in all the remaining diseases as well; and others sometimes take away the decline too, if the disease is resolved by 'abscission' (ex apokopēs), as they call it. First, then, these disputes must be settled; then the notions of the periods of the whole disease must be precisely articulated; after that their signs must be stated; and next it would remain to show their usefulness, combining it with what concerns the cycles. Now the beginning of the disease, insofar as it sets in at some moment when the healthy state collapses, is conceived in all of them without any extension of time. At the same time, however, it is not conceded that every disease has something like a genesis, such as we conceive in animals. For diseases are not composed of certain parts, as the animal is composed of head, thorax and limbs.

For, falling away [442] from the natural state, they have their coming-into-being in an instant of time, and from there they ascend up to the peak. For let the disease be, say, one consisting in a dyscrasia, the condition in which we have shown fever too to be constituted. It is necessary, then, that as soon as this unnatural heat first arises, the person is feverish, and that the heat is intensified up to the peak. 'For of that which has no parts, how could there be a coming-into-being in time?' These things were said by me right at the beginning as well, and I answered them by recalling the fevers that set in with chilling. But in the case of the periods the answer is sufficient; for the time of the chilling is one of the partial times of the whole disease, and the first in order. It would, however, be most ridiculous to regard the first time of the first paroxysm as the beginning of the whole disease. For this time, which they call the beginning of a disease, has its usefulness with respect to the remedies, and it was looking to this that he said: 'When diseases are beginning, if anything seems to need moving, move it; but when they are at their peak, it is better to keep quiet.'

In the same way he has also said this: [443] 'About the beginnings and the ends all things are weaker.' And moreover there is also what is said about purgation, that one should purge and set in motion what is concocted, not what is raw, nor at the beginnings, unless there is turgescence. And in addition to these there is further the saying, 'In acute affections use purgative medicines rarely and at the beginnings.' These, and many other things besides, said some by Hippocrates and others by all the other ancient physicians, do not permit us to understand the beginning as the onset of the first paroxysm. They require us to take it as extending over a longer span, long enough that one can perform phlebotomy and use a clyster, and sometimes, if it is urgent, also purge. Besides, it would be ridiculous to posit an equal beginning for diseases that are resolved within the seventh day and for those that persist for a year, as the quartan sometimes does. Much, then, has been said by me about this beginning also in the first book On Crises, where I showed how one might recognise this first period. Its chief point was the unconcoctedness of the disease. But it is better here too to say, in addition to those things, whatever is useful for the present exposition.

[444] Let it be laid down, then, first, that it is the beginning of an inflammation (phlegmonē) that is being sought. Who would not say that its quasi-generation, so to speak, lies in that whole time during which the part is being filled with blood-like substance? For whether this comes about by paremptōsis (intrusion), or by the wedging of all the vessels, or by some jamming of the corpuscles in the pores, or whether, as we have taught both in the treatise On Uneven Bad Temperament and in the treatise On Swellings Contrary to Nature, some excess of blood forms in the part while the inflammation is being generated, this will be the first period (kairos), in which the part is being filled, in proportion to the magnitude of the affection. But when what flows in has ceased, and what is contained in the inflamed part has begun to putrefy, a certain heat arises on account of the putrefaction, and the diffusion increases further on account of the heat, upon which pneuma is also generated; and through both of these the part is distended more than before, even if nothing should flow in. This is the second time, that of the increase of the inflammation.

When it is now changing into pus, then, I suppose, the greatest pains [445] take hold. For pains and fevers occur around the generation of pus rather than once it has been generated; and such a period is called the acme of the affection. But if the flux, by suppurating or by being dispersed, renders both the swelling and the tension smaller, this is the beginning of the decline. In this way, then, the periods are distinguished in the case of inflammation. In the case of fever, for a fever that arises upon an inflammation one is to posit the same periods as for the inflammation. For one that arises upon a humour without inflammation, the time of the lack of concoction of the troublesome humours is to be posited as the beginning. When they begin to be concocted, the beginning has ended and the second period has arrived, the one named that of the ascent. When the concoction itself is most fully being accomplished, that is the period of the acme. Then next comes that of the decline, in which both the magnitude of the symptoms and the quantity of the matters being concocted have already ceased, and there is still a small remnant of the humours that need to be concocted.

In my treatise On Crises I set out all the distinguishing signs as well: those of faint concoction and those of complete non-concoction, and those of evident concoction and those of perfect concoction, [446] some of them proper to the concoctions in the stomach, others to those in the veins, and others again to those of the respiratory parts. They were taken some from the stools, some from the urines, and some from the sputa. I went through these at very great length in that discussion, together with the Hippocratic passages; on the present occasion it is enough to say only this much: ulcers too have the same periods. For first watery, unconcocted and thin ichors flow from them; then next, ichors that are fewer and thicker; and after that, by now, thin pus; then this becomes less in quantity, but thicker and whiter. So there is none of the affections that are resolved which does not pass through the periods. Nor indeed does the recognition of them come from anything other than the signs of non-concoction and of concoction, which are recognised through the residues. For who does not know that the stomach has failed to concoct, when he has seen unchylified stools? And who does not know, when he has seen watery urine, that the concoction in the vessels has miscarried?

And who, having seen thin sputum coughed up in pleuritis or peripneumonia, will not likewise understand that it is still [447] the beginning of the affection? So too in ophthalmias: at the beginning there flows off much thin matter, quite unconcocted; next, less and thicker, taking on some trace of concoction; then, as time goes on, with the quantity diminishing and the consistency tending towards the thicker, the signs of concoction increase to such a degree that the eyelids of those who have slept are even glued together by the rheum that has formed. This rheum, too, is thin and abundant at the start, but with time becomes less and thicker, and so indicates both the concoction of the disease and its decline. Moreover, in the case of what flows down from the brain through the palate and the nostrils, it is the beginning when what is carried down is watery and thin and abundant and acrid, for these things indicate extreme non-concoction. The distinguishing marks of concoction, by now, are that the discharge is thicker and less acrid and is evacuated in small quantity. If what is called mucus and slime should also come away with it, this is already a surer sign of concoction; just as, indeed, (if) it becomes thicker and less abundant, it indicates concoction much more still. And these are the periods of diseases from which the sick are saved.

[448] As for the other times, those in which patients perish, I shall speak of them a little later, after first articulating whatever of what has been said requires some qualification. One of these is the question concerning the peak: whether it is always without duration, so far as it itself is concerned, even if to perception it often appears to be extended over considerable periods of time; or whether it always has some breadth, sometimes greater and sometimes less; or whether in some diseases it occupies a span of time and in others is without duration. But since the inquiry requires a longer discussion, I am inclined to pass over the whole of it, imitating Hippocrates, who said concerning dislocation at the shoulder: 'I do not, however, insist on this myself, although I have something to say.' For just as he was content with what he had always seen, in the same way I too shall now speak as one who has always seen it. Every peak of the individual paroxysms I have observed to take place over a span of time, so that even if by its nature it were without duration, we would derive no use from that fact.

For as soon as the decline first becomes clear to perception, we then use the remedies suited to it; [449] but so long as the magnitude of the fever stands at the same numbers, for so long it is proper to do what belongs to the magnitude of the peak. In the same way, in ophthalmia, pleuritis, every inflammation and each of the other diseases, the general periods, measured by perception, dictate the use of the different remedies. The inquiry into the breadth of the peak is therefore a logical one, whether one is considering something about the particular paroxysms or about the whole disease. But it is not my present purpose to distinguish such matters, as those do who bring everything into everything, among whom is Archigenes. For this man mixes into the most strictly medical treatises sometimes an inquiry about names, and at times also one about the things themselves, but a logical one. We, just as we have always guarded against this, shall do so now as well. Leaving it to others to inquire about the peak, whether it is timeless or occupies some time, we shall measure its use. For we see its nature plainly: among the ages of life, the age of prime runs its course over a broad span of time, and in diseases the peak runs its course sometimes over a longer span, often over a shorter one, but in every case over a perceptible one.

[450] This very difference of time is to be observed more clearly in animals, in the age of the prime. For indeed we see both hunting dogs and racing horses already performing something of their proper work in the period of growth. After this we say that they have become complete, and we see clearly that they are stronger than before, and that they keep the same strength not for one year only but sometimes for two and three years. So too human athletes remain of equal strength, as far as perception goes, not only for these three years but often for four and five. In the same way, as I said, in diseases too the individual paroxysms reach their peaks in a perceptible time. And much more do the general periods of the whole disease have breadth: both all the others, and that of the peak no less (is so) than each of the others. It is possible to recognise them sometimes clearly, sometimes dimly, or even to be entirely ignorant of them for a very long time.

And on this account some diseases seem to attack at once at their peak. Yet this very thing is among the impossibilities; for [451] not even the so-called synochus fever ever attacked straight from its peak; rather, from the first onset it reaches its most complete peak in four or three hours at the least, and from that point it remains entirely equal to itself, continuously, until the crisis. Nor would one say that the disease which attacks most suddenly of all, apoplexy, is at its peak; for such is not strictly the case. In a short time it passes through both the beginning and the ascent, yet it is certainly not without a beginning, nor does it attack at once in its most complete form, just as the paroxysm of epilepsy does not either. For no one is seized by the symptom as suddenly as those who have their neck severed; and yet even in their case the cutting has a first period of time, and a second, a third and a fourth, just as when a surgeon cuts anything whatever. But, if you wish, let it be granted that both the epileptic and the apoplectic falling-down occur without time, so that I may go through what I proposed at the outset.

For the collapse that occurs is itself a symptom, but the disease is not this; rather it must by all means, as we have demonstrated, be some condition [452] of the body. And if we have no sign of it either while it is being generated or while it is increasing, this does not overturn the consequent argument, according to which we said that it is necessary for every disease to arrive at the acme through the increase; rather, it concedes that the growth of diseases is sometimes hard to recognise, and in many of them unrecognisable. That what I say is true, I could persuade you with this very brief argument. I have often seen scirrhous swellings in the legs forming straightaway from the beginning, without inflammation having preceded them, and growing little by little, sometimes for three and even four years, without perceptibly impeding the necessary functions of the leg; but in the course of time, on account of their considerable size, at some later point they also troubled walking.

Conceive, then (for it is not impossible), that some scirrhous swelling is already forming in the concave parts of the liver. Its formation will escape notice up to a certain point. Later, however, the features of the condition itself will become more evident, though even then we are unable to discover upon what condition this ensues. At a still later time a dropsical effusion [453] will at some point also occur, while even then the scirrhous swelling gives no distinct sign to the touch. But having later become manifest, and of considerable size, it reminded us of our earlier ignorance. At any rate, I myself have seen not a few patients who, by such a course of the symptoms, showed within a short time a swelling of no small size in a scirrhous liver. It had been forming for a long time but escaped notice because of its own smallness and the good nourishment of the muscles in the hypochondrium. But when the scirrhus, as it grows, at once mounts up onto the convex parts of the liver and at the same time becomes a cause of lack of nourishment both to the other parts of the animal and to the muscles in the hypochondrium, then from both of these you will clearly diagnose it within a short time, since it has by then reached a considerable size. All such matters belong to the inquiry into the affected parts, which it is not our present purpose to examine; but they have been set out, not without use, because of their connection with it. It is time to return to the original argument.

Each of the diseases has its own proper period of origination, sometimes perceptible, sometimes not perceptible; after which, in turn, the period of increase is not perceptible in the same way in [454] all cases, not even this one. These are followed by the period of the peak, which is in every case perceptible, although we grant that sometimes there is no clear mark of the beginning of the affection and of its increase. In these cases, then, so far as the use of the art is concerned, one will truly say that only the time of the peak exists; and, if the patients are going to be saved, that the period of the decline necessarily follows it, and this too is perceptible, since it is constituted in a time that is not without extension. For even if someone has an acute crisis, whether through a haemorrhage or through sweats, there is at any rate some period of decline in this case too, and a perceptible one. And if in other diseases this occurs to a lesser degree, the disease declining over three or four or even more days, this plainly does no harm to the preceding argument, nor does it discredit the chief point of the assertion; rather, it still stands that all diseases that are resolved have, just as a peak, so also some decline. These things having been sufficiently demonstrated by us, we shall next examine the diseases that are not resolved.

Their nature is twofold. For some of them have the constitution [sc. of fatal diseases?] [455] whenever they have it brought exactly to completion; others are of the nature of those that are resolved, but when [the disease] kills first, it is in this respect that this happens to them. And of these too the manner is threefold: for they carry off [the patient] before being resolved either because of the patient's want of strength, or because of the strength of the diseases, or because of both together. But on another account there is one common pattern for all such cases, namely when [the disease] is beyond the strength. For the very cause that sustains the patient's destruction is set in this: no one can be saved unless nature masters the disease, nor perish without nature being defeated and the disease becoming more powerful than it. And for this reason some think that a single thing is signified by 'great disease', as though it consisted in a relation to something. They do not know that 'great disease' is sometimes said in this way, just as if we were also to say 'greater', when it is beyond the strength. But it is also said with reference to its own proper substance, as a man, or a horse, or an ox is called great.

This double meaning, too, has already been demonstrated by me many times in other works; but to work out everything in every work is [456] idle prattle. What is useful for the present purposes, then, is what I shall state. Each of the diseases in and by itself possesses a certain magnitude (for it is better to put it thus for the sake of clarity), and this magnitude of the disease is either beyond the strength, so as to weigh it down, or, on the contrary, weaker than the strength, so as to be overcome by it, provided that everything is done properly. When, then, it is beyond the strength, the person will certainly die. The periods of the disease in that case are taken in one respect in the same way as those stated before, but in another respect not in the same way. For the beginning has its constitution in the same manner, in the coming-to-be of the disease; but the increase lies not in the being concocted, as in the case of those who are going to be saved, but in the signs of non-concoction and in the deadly signs. For it was shown, if we remember anything, that these differ from one another; and for the sake of reminder some of them will be stated now as well.

Now the urine that is of good colour and moderately thick is the finest of all urines, so far as colour and consistency are concerned. But there must by all means be present together with it either a favourable suspended matter, [457] or a cloud, or a sediment, as the nature of the disease may demand. For we have shown that sediments come about in one way in bilious diseases and in another way in plethoras arising from crude humours. At the diametrically opposite extreme, as one might say, is the unconcocted urine, which has neither suspended matter nor sediment nor cloud, and has not even taken on any thickness or yellowness, but is white in colour and thin in consistency, like water. If, however, some cloud, or a black suspended matter, or a black sediment should form in it, and still more if the whole of it should be murky, it is deadly; just as it is also if things like coarse meal or like flakes should appear in it. And indeed urine that is strongly foul-smelling is also deadly, and so is the greasy urine, which they call oily. These, then, are the urines that are distinguishing marks of a great disease, that is, of one which, as I was saying, is great by its own nature.

And [the disease is] great also if, in pleuritics and peripneumonics, the sputum is either black, or intensely tawny, or frothy, or considerably foul-smelling, or is not brought up at all, while violent pain or dyspnoea [458] grips the patient. Analogous to these, in the other diseases as well, those that arise in the liver or the stomach, there exists a class of deadly signs. Hence it is not possible to define the acme in such diseases in the same way as the acme of those who are going to be saved. For there the greatest paroxysms marked off the acme, but here one cannot define the greatest ones in the same way, since the disease is not being concocted at all. Rather, one must grasp by conception the greatest [extent], which the disease sometimes reaches, while at other times it kills [the patient] before reaching it. In the case of an inflammation that is being resolved, the generation of pus is the boundary of the acme. In the case of one that is not going to be resolved, it is possible for the patient to die even during its ascent, but it is also possible for the strength, if it is very powerful, to hold out until the final magnitude. For the greatest magnitude of this inflammation, whenever it is not going to be resolved, ends either in gangrene or in putrefaction; and so long as it is not yet either of these, it can increase.

And analogously to inflammation let the [459] increases in each kind of the other diseases also be understood. Not only their kinds, but also their differentiae and species, have been set out in a single treatise, which is entitled On the Differences of Diseases. But I ask you to pay particular attention to the following point, which, if overlooked, could badly mislead someone. For it is possible for a person to be afflicted at one and the same time by two or even three diseases, of which one is already in decline, another still remains in the period of its beginning, or in the first stages of its ascent, and another has increased to the greatest extent; and then for the person to die neither on account of the one in decline, nor on account of the one now beginning, but on account of the one that has greatly increased. Above all, therefore, examine how the three principles of the faculties that govern the whole body are disposed; I mean these: brain, heart and liver. Next, examine also all the other parts: those that grow from each of the principles, namely nerves, veins and arteries, and whatever parts have a nature of their own but are governed by all the principles, some equally, others more by one and less by another.

[460] For from such a study you will first find out whether there is one disease, or several diseases, in the person; then, next, examine the proper times of each, since these are necessary for the discovery of the remedies, for the sake of which this discourse is being earnestly pursued by us. For around the beginnings and the ends all things are weaker, around the peaks stronger, and in between these they are intermediate. For those nearer to the beginning are weaker than those nearer to the peak, just as are also those nearer to the end; and those equally distant from the beginning and from the peak are intermediate in strength between both extremes; and so likewise those equally distant from the peak and from the end, these too are intermediate between their own extremes.

It is fitting, then, that in therapy the palliative should predominate at the peak, and the combative at the beginning and at the end; and the intermediate periods are to be taken in proportion to the extremes, as has been said at greater length in the treatise on the therapeutic method. Now, by way of an outline, I have gone through only the main headings themselves, showing the usefulness of the distinction in diseases according to [461] periods. For it is not possible to discover either how one will regulate the diet or when one will feed, without determining these securely, if indeed one must infer right from the beginning both when the peak of the disease will come and how great the strength of the patient is. For if it will hold out through the time of the peak even without taking food, it is best to fast until the decline has begun; but if he cannot last out while fasting, he must be fed right from the beginning at every period able to receive food, and this is the period of remission. By remission I mean here the second part of the whole period, when the whole is divided into two, paroxysm and remission. Hippocrates, then, first of all those we know of, made correct determinations about this; but it would have been better to work out his art more fully. Yet almost no one did this, and some, departing from it altogether, turned aside into prolixity, as Archigenes did both in all his other writings and in the two books which he wrote on the periods in diseases.

You will learn clearly what I mean once you have examined these two things precisely: [462] first, whether the things now stated by us throughout this whole book are most useful for therapy and prognosis; second, whether anything has been said by Archigenes. For if, although nothing is lacking in these, he evidently says other things, he errs in two ways: he does not teach what is useful, and he burdens those who read his books with the verbosity of useless matters.
